title: Akkusativ vs. Dativ
theoryMd:
German marks the **role** a noun plays in a sentence by changing the article in front of it. The two cases you will use constantly are the **accusative** (the direct object) and the **dative** (the indirect object). Getting them right is mostly a matter of asking one question and knowing three short lists.

## The one question that decides it

For most verbs, ask: **wen oder was?** (whom or what?) → accusative. **wem?** (to whom?) → dative.

- *Ich sehe **den Mann**.* — I see whom? The man. → accusative.
- *Ich helfe **dem Mann**.* — I help to whom? The man. → dative.

English hides this because it uses word order instead. In *I give the man the book*, English tells you *the man* is the recipient purely by position. German tells you with the article: *Ich gebe **dem Mann** **das Buch**.*

## The forms

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nominative** | der / ein | die / eine | das / ein | die / — |
| **accusative** | **den / einen** | die / eine | das / ein | die / — |
| **dative** | **dem / einem** | **der / einer** | **dem / einem** | **den / — (+n)** |

Two observations save you a lot of memorising:

1. **Only masculine changes in the accusative.** *der → den*, *ein → einen*. Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly like the nominative. So if the noun is not masculine, the accusative costs you nothing.
2. **The dative plural adds -n to the noun itself**: *die Kinder → mit den Kinder**n***, *die Freunde → mit den Freunde**n***. If the plural already ends in -n or -s, nothing changes.

The feminine dative *der* is the form that trips learners up, because it looks like a masculine nominative. *Ich helfe der Frau* — that *der* is dative feminine, not masculine.

## Verbs that always take the dative

This is a closed list, and it is short enough to learn outright. These verbs take a dative object where English would suggest a direct one:

- **helfen** — *Ich helfe dir.* (I help you)
- **danken** — *Ich danke Ihnen.* (I thank you)
- **gehören** — *Das gehört mir.* (That belongs to me)
- **gefallen** — *Der Film gefällt mir.* (I like the film)
- **antworten** — *Ich antworte dem Lehrer.*
- **folgen** — *Folgen Sie mir.*
- **glauben** — *Ich glaube dir.*
- **passen**, **schmecken**, **fehlen**, **gratulieren**

*Gefallen* is worth a second look because it inverts the English subject: the thing that pleases is the **subject**, and the person is in the dative. *Mir gefällt das Buch* — literally "to me pleases the book".

## Prepositions: three groups

Prepositions decide the case of whatever follows them, and they fall into three groups.

**Always accusative:** *durch, für, gegen, ohne, um*

> *Ich gehe **durch den** Park. Das ist **für dich**.*

**Always dative:** *aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu* (and *gegenüber*)

> *Ich fahre **mit dem** Bus. Ich komme **aus der** Schweiz.*

**Two-way (Wechselpräpositionen):** *an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen*

These take **accusative for movement towards a place**, and **dative for a static location**. The test is: *wohin?* (where to?) → accusative; *wo?* (where?) → dative.

| Movement (wohin? → accusative) | Position (wo? → dative) |
|---|---|
| Ich gehe **in die** Küche. | Ich bin **in der** Küche. |
| Er legt das Buch **auf den** Tisch. | Das Buch liegt **auf dem** Tisch. |
| Sie hängt das Bild **an die** Wand. | Das Bild hängt **an der** Wand. |

A useful pair of verbs to anchor this: **legen/liegen**, **stellen/stehen**, **setzen/sitzen**, **hängen/hängen**. The first of each pair is an action with a direct object and takes the accusative; the second is a state and takes the dative.

## Putting both objects together

When a sentence has both a dative and an accusative object, the default order is **dative before accusative**:

> *Ich gebe **dem Kind** **den Ball**.*

But if the accusative object is a **pronoun**, it jumps in front:

> *Ich gebe **ihn** **dem Kind**.* (I give it to the child)

And with two pronouns, accusative comes first: *Ich gebe **ihn ihm**.*

> A shortcut worth internalising: **nouns keep dative-first, pronouns force accusative-first.**

payload.explanation: sehen takes a direct object → accusative. Masculine der becomes den.
helfen is one of the dative verbs, so the object is dative: dem Mann.
mit is always dative. Masculine dative is dem.
für is always accusative. Feminine accusative looks like the nominative: meine Freundin.
in is a two-way preposition. Movement towards → accusative: in die Küche.
Static location → dative. Feminine dative is der: in der Küche.

payload.hint: wo? — the book is not moving
payload.explanation: liegen describes a state, so the two-way preposition auf takes the dative: auf dem Tisch.

payload.prompt: Er legt das Buch auf ___ Tisch.
payload.hint: wohin? — the book is being moved
payload.explanation: legen is an action moving something, so auf takes the accusative: auf den Tisch.
gefallen takes a dative person: Der Film gefällt mir = I like the film. The film is the subject.
The dative plural adds -n to the noun itself: mit den Kindern.

payload.prompt: gebe / dem Kind / ich / den Ball
answers: Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball
payload.explanation: With two noun objects the order is dative before accusative: dem Kind (to whom) then den Ball (what).

distractors: Ich gebe ihm den Ball ihn.
payload.explanation: A pronoun object jumps ahead of a noun object, so the accusative pronoun ihn comes before dem Kind.
